_comment: Caption text per beat, taken from fielding_video_script_v4.md. Timing inside each beat is spread evenly by text length, so re-time in your editor if you ad-libbed. Used by tools/make_srt.py.
01_open: Two runs off. But fielding is where I can't tell you the whole story. I'm building CricPredict: a cricket prediction app for fans. Entertainment only, not betting.
02_moments: First ODI of India's 2026 tour of New Zealand. Virat Kohli took a one-handed diving catch at second slip to dismiss Nathan Smith. Rohit Sharma made a sharp run-out assist. Moments like these swing a match.
03_84_4: At 84 for four after 17 overs, CricPredict predicted 199 for seven.
04_finished: New Zealand finished 185 all out: fourteen runs lower, but three wickets more than predicted.
05_171_9: Later, at 171 for nine after 37.3 overs, it predicted 183 all out.
06_183: Two runs off. Encouraging, but a much shorter forecasting horizon.
07_mae: Did fielding explain the gap? I can't prove it. But the model has room to improve: in my backtest on men's ODIs, its average error is 41.5 runs.
08_hand: Fielding is one thing it can't see properly. Today it is just one hand-assigned rating per team, a reputation, not who is actually on the field.
08b_hold: I think that is part of what's holding accuracy back, on runs and on wickets.
09_public: Public ball-by-ball data only names a fielder when a wicket falls. No drops, no misfields, no dives, no runs saved.
10_plan: So here is the plan. Start with what public data does give me, the catches and run-outs that end in a wicket, and build a first fielding model from that in shadow mode, knowing its limits. Then, if I can get ball-by-ball fielding data, use it to rate the actual fielders in each XI. Test the effect on runs and wickets separately, on fresh matches. If it doesn't beat the current model, it doesn't ship.
11_ask: If you hold fielding data, or work at a data provider, message me. Try CricPredict at cricket-score-predictor.com.
